items.title: Solving Systems Containing Perfect Square Quadratics

sections.normalized_html: In the [MATH: xy]-plane, what is the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the point of intersection of the graphs of [MATH: y = (x - 12)^2] and [MATH: y = 24x - 432?]
sections.readable_text: In the [MATH: xy]-plane, what is the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the point of intersection of the graphs of [MATH: y = (x - 12)^2] and [MATH: y = 24x - 432?]

sections.normalized_html:
To find the coordinates of the point of intersection, we need to solve the following system of equations: [MATH: {y = (x − 12)^{2}; y = 24x − 432]

Since both equations are solved for [MATH: y,] we set them equal and put in standard form:

[MATH: (x − 12)^{2}|= 24x − 432; x^{2} − 24x + 144|= 24x − 432; x^{2} − 48x + 576|= 0]

Now, notice that the left-hand side is a perfect square. It just needs to be factored: [MATH: x^{2} − 48x + 576|= 0; x^{2} − 2 ⋅ 24 ⋅ x + 24^{2}|= 0; (x − 24)^{2}|= 0]

Applying the zero product rule yields [MATH: x=24,] and so we substitute [MATH: x = 24] into either equation to find the corresponding [MATH: y]-value. We use [MATH: y = 24x - 432{:}]

[MATH: y|= 24x − 432; = 24(24) − 432; = 576 − 432; = 144]

Therefore, the value of [MATH: y] is [MATH: 144.]

items.title: Solving Systems by Factoring a Common Binomial

sections.normalized_html:
[MATH: {y = (x + 3)(x − 6); y = 9x − 54]

What is the ordered pair [MATH: (x, y)] that satisfies the given system of equations?
sections.readable_text:
[MATH: {y = (x + 3)(x − 6); y = 9x − 54]

What is the ordered pair [MATH: (x, y)] that satisfies the given system of equations?

sections.normalized_html:
First, we write both equations of the given system in factored form: [MATH: {y = (x + 3)(x − 6); y = 9(x − 6)]

Notice that [MATH: x-6] is a common factor in both equations. To find the solution, we set the two expressions for [MATH: y] equal to each other and factor:

[MATH: (x + 3)(x − 6)|= 9(x − 6); (x + 3)(x − 6) − 9(x − 6)|= 0; (x − 6)[(x + 3) − 9]|= 0; (x − 6)(x − 6)|= 0; (x − 6)^{2}|= 0]

Applying the zero product rule then yields

[MATH: x − 6|= 0; x|= 6.]

Finally, we substitute [MATH: x = 6] into either equation to find the corresponding [MATH: y]-value. Using [MATH: y = 9(x - 6),] we obtain

[MATH: y|= 9(x − 6); = 9(6 − 6); = 9(0); = 0.]

Therefore, the solution to the system is [MATH: (6, 0).]
